newsitem.title: USA: California gets electric deregulation bill.
newsitem.headline: California gets electric deregulation bill.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson on Monday signed far-reaching legislation to open the state's $21 billion electricity market to competition and slash consumer rates by 20 percent by the year 2002.

"We're doing more than signing a new law, we are shifting the balance of power in California," Wilson, a Republican, said at the bill signing ceremony in San Diego. "We've pulled the plug on another outdated monopoly and replaced it with the promise of a new era of competition."
The legislation makes "California the first state in the nation to dismantle its electric monopoloy," Wilson said.

The state Legislature approved the deregulation plan in late August. Lawmakers described the measure as historic and a model for the nation since dozens of other states are considering similar proposals.

The sweeping measure will restructure the electric industry in California, ending the utility monopoly on generation and opening the market to competition so that retail customers can choose among electric energy suppliers.
The bill has the support of the large utilities that would be affected most, Pacific Gas and Electric Co., San Diego Gas and Electric and Southern California Edison.

"We believe competition is good for consumers and businesses throughout California, for our industry and for the California economy," said Donald Felsinger, president and chief executive officer of San Diego Gas and Electric.

Wilson said deregulation would stimulate the state's economy, save schools more than $123 million by the year 2002, ensure a reliable source of power and provide safeguards against widespread power outages.
Critics said the plan was a bailout for utilities.
The legislation lays out a five-year transition period during which the industry will be opened to competition.
Residential users and small commercial businesses are guaranteed a rate reduction of 10 percent starting Jan. 1, 1998, followed by another 10 percent reduction by 2002.
Currently, California's electrical rates are 40 percent higher than the national average -- 50 percent higher than Texas, 65 percent higher than Nevada and 120 percent higher than Oregon.

To help the investor-owned utilities better compete as the power generation market opens, the utilities will be compensated for certain "stranded" costs, such as nuclear power plants, that would not be economical in a competitive market.
The legislation authorizes the California Infrastructure Bank to issue up to $10 billion in revenue bonds to help the utilities pay off their stranded costs.
By issuing the bonds through the state bank, the utilities will obtain more favorable interest rates on the debt. State taxpayers would have no obligation or financial exposure.
The bond financings will provide substantial savings to the utilities, which will be passed on to the customers.

Following the bill signing, Standard & Poor's Corp. revised its ratings outlook for Southern California Edison to stable from negative. S&P also revised Pacific Gas and Electric to positive from negative and San Diego Gas and Electric to stable from negative.
"It's a positive development," said S&P Director Cheryl Richer of the legislation. "If they (the utilities) use cash to pay down debt, they should emerge with very strong financials."
